children: British arrived in India as traders in 1600
East India Company granted exclusive trading rights by charter from Queen Elizabeth I
Court of Directors was the governing body of the Company

concepts.text: Company obtained Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (1765)
children: Diwani gave Company rights over revenue and civil justice
Company's career as a territorial power began from 1765
Mughal Emperor Shah Alam granted Diwani after Company's victory in Battle of Buxar (1764)
Battle of Buxar (1764) led to the grant of Diwani
First step by British Government to control and regulate affairs of East India Company
First recognition of political and administrative functions of the Company
Laid foundations of central administration in India
Designated Governor of Bengal as Governor-General of Bengal
Created an Executive Council of four members to assist the Governor-General
First Governor-General of Bengal: Lord Warren Hastings
Made governors of Bombay and Madras presidencies subordinate to Governor-General of Bengal (earlier independent)
Establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 comprising one chief justice and three other judges
Prohibited servants of Company from engaging in private trade and from accepting presents or bribes from natives
Strengthened control of British Government by requiring Court of Directors to report on revenue, civil, and military affairs
Purpose: rectify defects of Regulating Act of 1773
Exempted Governor-General and Council from Supreme Court jurisdiction for official acts
Exempted servants of Company from Supreme Court jurisdiction for official actions
Excluded revenue matters from Supreme Court jurisdiction
Supreme Court had jurisdiction over all inhabitants of Calcutta
Supreme Court required to administer personal law of defendants (Hindus by Hindu law, Muslims by Mohammedan law)
Appeals from Provincial Courts could go to Governor-General-in-Council, not Supreme Court
Empowered Governor-General-in-Council to frame regulations for Provincial Courts and Councils
Introduced by British Prime Minister William Pitt
Distinguished between commercial and political functions of the Company
Court of Directors allowed to manage commercial affairs
Created Board of Control to manage political affairs
Established system of double government
Board of Control empowered to supervise all civil, military and government operations in British possessions in India
Company's territories called 'British possessions in India' for first time
British Government given supreme control over Company's affairs and administration in India
Lord Cornwallis appointed Governor-General of Bengal in 1786
Empowered to override his council in special cases
Allowed Lord Cornwallis to also serve as Commander-in-Chief
Extended overriding power to all future Governor-Generals and Governors of Presidencies
Gave Governor-General more powers over subordinate Presidencies of Bombay and Madras
Extended Company's trade monopoly in India for another twenty years
Commander-in-Chief not to be a member of Governor-General's council unless appointed
Members of Board of Control and staff to be paid out of Indian revenues
Abolished Company's trade monopoly in India except for tea and trade with China
Asserted sovereignty of British Crown over Company's territories in India
Allowed Christian missionaries to come to India for enlightening the people
Provided for spread of western education among inhabitants of British territories in India
Authorised Local Governments in India to impose taxes on persons and punish for non-payment
Final step towards centralisation in British India
Made Governor-General of Bengal as Governor-General of India
Vested in Governor-General of India all civil and military powers
Created Government of India for the first time having authority over entire British Indian territory
First Governor-General of India: Lord William Bentick
Deprived Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers
Governor-General given exclusive legislative powers for entire British India
Laws made previously called Regulations; under this Act called Acts
Ended East India Company as a commercial body; became purely administrative
Company's territories held 'in trust for His Majesty, His heirs and successors'
Attempted to introduce open competition for selection of civil servants
Stated Indians should not be debarred from holding any office under the Company (provision later negated)
Last of the series of Charter Acts between 1793 and 1853
Significant constitutional landmark
Separated legislative and executive functions of Governor-General's council for the first time
Added six new members called legislative councillors
Established a separate Governor-General's legislative council known as Indian (Central) Legislative Council
Legislative wing functioned as a mini-Parliament adopting same procedures as British Parliament
Introduced open competition system for selection and recruitment of civil servants
Covenanted civil service thrown open to Indians
Macaulay Committee on Indian Civil Service appointed in 1854
Extended Company's rule but could be terminated anytime by Parliament
Introduced local representation: four of six new legislative members appointed by provincial governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra
Enacted in wake of the Revolt of 1857 (First War of Independence / Sepoy Mutiny)
Known as the Act for the Good Government of India
Abolished East India Company
Transferred powers of government, territories and revenues to British Crown
India to be governed by and in the name of Her Majesty
Changed designation of Governor-General of India to Viceroy of India
Viceroy as direct representative of British Crown in India
Lord Canning became first Viceroy of India
Ended system of double government by abolishing Board of Control and Court of Directors
Created new office: Secretary of State for India (member of British Cabinet)
Established a 15-member Council of India (advisory body) to assist Secretary of State
Secretary of State made Chairman of the Council
Constituted Secretary of State-in-Council as a body corporate capable of suing and being sued
Act largely confined to improvement of administrative machinery in England; did not alter Indian government substantially
Policy of association after 1857 revolt: sought cooperation of Indians in administration
Important landmark: began representative institutions by associating Indians with law-making
Viceroy to nominate some Indians as non-official members of his expanded council
In 1862, Lord Canning nominated three Indians (Raja of Benaras, Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao)
Initiated process of decentralisation by restoring legislative powers to Bombay and Madras Presidencies
Reversed centralising tendency that started with Regulating Act of 1773 and climaxed under Charter Act of 1833
Policy of legislative devolution led to grant of almost complete internal autonomy to provinces in 1937
Provided for establishment of new legislative councils for Bengal (1862), North-Western Provinces (1886), and Punjab (1897)
Empowered Viceroy to make rules for convenient transaction of business in council
Gave recognition to portfolio system introduced by Lord Canning in 1859 (member in-charge of one or more departments)
Empowered Viceroy to issue ordinances without legislative council concurrence during emergency (life: six months)
Increased number of additional (non-official) members in Central and provincial legislative councils
Maintained official majority in legislative councils
Increased functions: power to discuss budget and address questions to executive
Provided for nomination of some non-official members of Central Legislative Council on recommendation of provincial councils and Bengal Chamber of Commerce
Provided for nomination of non-official members of provincial councils on recommendation of district boards, municipalities, universities, trade associations, zamindars and chambers
Limited and indirect provision for use of election in filling some non-official seats (word 'election' not used)
Lord Morley (Secretary of State) and Lord Minto (Viceroy)
Considerably increased size of Central legislative council from 16 to 60
Retained official majority in Central legislative council
Allowed provincial legislative councils to have non-official majority
Enlarged deliberative functions: members allowed to ask supplementary questions, move resolutions on budget
Provided for association of Indians with executive councils of Viceroy and Governors for the first time
Satyendra Prasad Sinha became first Indian to join Viceroy's executive council as Law Member
Introduced system of communal representation for Muslims by accepting concept of 'separate electorate' (Muslims elected only by Muslim voters)
Act 'legalised communalism'; Lord Minto known as Father of Communal Electorate
Provided for separate representation of presidency corporations, chambers of commerce, universities and zamindars

concepts.text: Government of India Act of 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)
children: Based on British Government declaration of August 20, 1917 promising gradual introduction of responsible government
Montagu (Secretary of State) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy)
Act came into force in 1921
Relaxed central control by demarcating and separating central and provincial subjects
Central and provincial legislatures authorised to make laws on respective lists
Structure of government continued to be centralised and unitary
Further divided provincial subjects into transferred and reserved
Transferred subjects administered by Governor with ministers responsible to legislative council
Reserved subjects administered by Governor and executive council without being responsible to legislature
Dual scheme known as 'dyarchy' (from Greek di-arche meaning double rule); largely unsuccessful
Introduced bicameralism at Centre for the first time (Council of State - Upper House, Legislative Assembly - Lower House)
Introduced direct elections for the first time; majority of members chosen by direct election
Required three of six members of Viceroy's executive Council (other than Commander-in-Chief) to be Indian
Extended principle of communal representation with separate electorates for Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans
Granted franchise to limited number on basis of property, tax or education
Created new office of High Commissioner for India in London; transferred some functions from Secretary of State
Provided for establishment of a public service commission; Central Public Service Commission set up in 1926
Lee Commission (1923-24) recommended formation of the Public Service Commission
Separated provincial budgets from Central budget for the first time; provinces authorised to enact their budgets
Provided for appointment of a statutory commission after ten years (led to Simon Commission)
Announced November 1927: seven-member statutory commission under chairmanship of Sir John Simon
All members were British; all parties boycotted the commission
Submitted its report in 1930
Recommended abolition of dyarchy
Recommended extension of responsible government in provinces
Recommended establishment of a federation of British India and princely states
Recommended continuation of communal electorate
Three round table conferences convened by British Government to consider constitutional proposals
Representatives of British Government, British India and Indian princely states attended
A 'White Paper on Constitutional Reforms' prepared on basis of discussions
White Paper submitted to Joint Select Committee of British Parliament
Recommendations of Joint Select Committee incorporated (with changes) in Government of India Act of 1935
August 1932: British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced scheme of representation of minorities (Communal Award)
Continued separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans
Extended separate electorates to depressed classes (Scheduled Castes)
Gandhiji distressed over extension to depressed classes; fasted unto death in Yerawada Jail
Agreement between Congress leaders and depressed classes: Poona Pact
Poona Pact retained Hindu joint electorate but gave reserved seats to depressed classes
Second milestone towards completely responsible government in India
Lengthy and detailed document with 321 Sections and 10 Schedules
Provided for establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states (never implemented because princely states did not join)
Divided powers between Centre and units in three lists: Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54 items), Concurrent List (36 items); residuary powers to Viceroy
Abolished dyarchy in provinces; introduced provincial autonomy
Provinces allowed to act as autonomous units in defined spheres; Governor required to act on advice of ministers responsible to provincial legislature
Provincial autonomy came into effect in 1937 but discontinued in 1939
Provided for adoption of dyarchy at Centre (federal subjects divided into reserved and transferred) but never came into operation
Introduced bicameralism in six out of eleven provinces: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, United Provinces (legislative council and legislative assembly)
Many restrictions placed on provincial legislatures
Further extended principle of communal representation with separate electorates for depressed classes, women and labour (workers)
Abolished Council of India established by Act of 1858; Secretary of State provided with a team of advisors
Extended franchise to about 10% of total population
Provided for establishment of Reserve Bank of India, Federal Public Service Commission, Provincial Public Service Commissions, Joint Public Service Commissions
Provided for establishment of a Federal Court (set up in 1937)
February 20, 1947: British PM Clement Atlee declared British rule would end by June 30, 1948
Agitation by Muslim League demanding partition of the country
June 3, 1947: British Government made clear any Constitution framed by Constituent Assembly (1946) cannot apply to parts unwilling to accept
Same day: Lord Mountbatten (Viceroy) put forth partition plan known as Mountbatten Plan; accepted by Congress and Muslim League
Act gave immediate effect: ended British rule; India declared independent and sovereign from August 15, 1947
Provided for partition of India into two independent dominions: India and Pakistan
Right of dominions to secede from British Commonwealth
Abolished office of Viceroy; each dominion to have a Governor-General appointed by British King on advice of dominion cabinet
His Majesty's Government in Britain no responsibility for India or Pakistan
Empowered Constituent Assemblies to frame constitutions, legislate for their territories, and repeal any British Act including this Act
No Act of British Parliament after August 15, 1947 to extend to either dominion unless adopted by dominion legislature
Abolished office of Secretary of State for India; functions transferred to Secretary of State for Commonwealth Affairs
Proclaimed lapse of British paramountcy over Indian princely states and treaty relations with tribal areas from August 15, 1947
Princely states granted freedom to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent
Government of India Act of 1935 to govern each dominion and provinces till new constitutions framed; dominions could make modifications
Deprived British Monarch of right to veto bills; Governor-General reserved right to veto or ask for reservation
Governor-General and provincial governors designated constitutional (nominal) heads acting on advice of council of ministers
Dropped title of Emperor of India from royal titles of King of England
Discontinued appointment to civil services by Secretary of State; existing members retained benefits
Boundaries determined by Boundary Commission under Radcliff; Pakistan included West Punjab, Sind, Baluchistan, East Bengal, NWFP and Sylhet
At midnight August 14-15, 1947, power transferred to two dominions; Lord Mountbatten became first Governor-General of India
Lord Mountbatten swore in Jawaharlal Nehru as first Prime Minister of independent India
Constituent Assembly of India (formed 1946) became Parliament of Indian Dominion
Members of interim government were members of Viceroy's Executive Council; Viceroy continued as head; Jawaharlal Nehru designated Vice-President

Features of Indian Constitution and polity rooted in British rule
System of Budget introduced in British India in 1860
